To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) logging debris and competing-vegetative cover are sources of dissolved C and dissolved N in the soil solution; and 2) the magnitude of dissolved C and nitrogen loss is greater in treatments that retain logging debris and that receive annual applications of competing-vegetation herbicide.
annual CVC increased nitrate-N concentration in soil water, but did not result in increased leaching loss.
Annual competing-vegetation removal increased soil water nitrate concentrations and fluxes, but had no effect on soil water DOC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of competing-vegetation removal and retention of logging debris on dissolved C and N leaching in Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii (Mirbel) Franco) plantations of western OR and WA.
the effects of logging debris and competing-vegetative species on the fate of carbon and nitrogen in forest soil.

the effects of logging debris retention and competing vegetation control on soil water nitrate, dissolved organic carbon, and dissolved organic nitrogen leaching from two sites in the western Cascade Mountains of Oregon and Washington.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of annual CVC on dissolved organic nitrogen was the only effect of any of the treatments that was significant.
annual CVC increased soil water nitrate flux at both sites, with a greater effect on nitrate flux at the high-N soil.
logging-debris retention has no measurable effect on DOC and N leaching and that the effect of competing vegetation on DOC and N is site dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

annual competing-vegetation con- trol (CVC) increased dissolved organic N and nitrate-N flux, and logging-debris retention increased nitrate-N flux at a low-N site, with little effect on dissolved organic C or N flux.
the effects of logging-debris and competing-vegetative control on soil water chemistry were small relative to the magnitude of the soil pools of these elements.
the potential for increased soil water N leaching from Douglas-fir plantings is low, and that the potential for loss of DOC and DON is even less.
The main takeaway from our work is that
annual CVC can increase soil water nitrate fluxes, particularly at low-N sites.
logging debris retention and competing- vegetation control do not increase soil water C and N leaching.
annual CVC can lead to increases in soil water nitrate leaching at sites where N availability is high.
